intro.title: How ready is your business for AI?
intro.text: Answer honestly; there are no wrong answers. Most small businesses score in the middle, and every result comes with practical next steps.
bullets: The two areas to focus on first, with free resources

dims.name: Processes
dims.advice: Write down the steps for your two most common workflows, agree on how exceptions are handled, and remove steps that only exist because of old tools.
link: Lesson: mapping a process before you automate it

dims.name: Data
dims.advice: Pick one system as the source of truth for customers, make key fields required, and merge duplicates. Clean data makes automation and AI far more reliable.
link: Guide: how to automate data entry

dims.name: Tools and integrations
dims.advice: List your core apps and check what integrations and APIs each one offers. Replacing one closed tool is sometimes the biggest unlock.

dims.name: People and ownership
dims.advice: Name an owner, give them a few hours a week, and involve the people who do the work today. Frame automation as removing chores, not jobs.

dims.name: Goals and guardrails
dims.advice: Choose one process and one metric to improve, and write a short policy on which AI tools are approved and what data they may see.

bands.title: Getting started
bands.text: You are at the beginning, which is a perfectly good place to be. Your fastest wins will come from documenting one or two key processes and getting customer data into one place. Start with a simple, rule-based automation before adding AI.

bands.title: Building foundations
bands.text: Some of the pieces are in place. Shore up the weakest areas below, pick one specific process with a clear goal, and you will be ready for a first automation, with AI steps wherever reading or writing is involved.

bands.title: Ready to pilot
bands.text: You are ready for a focused pilot. Choose one high-volume process, decide how you will measure success, and build it end to end, adding AI where it handles language or judgment and keeping a person in the loop at first.

bands.title: Ready to scale
bands.text: Your processes, data, and team are in good shape. You can automate several workflows and use AI more ambitiously, including agents for well-scoped tasks with clear guardrails. The main risk now is sprawl, so keep ownership and monitoring clear.

explainer:
What this AI readiness assessment measures

AI and automation succeed or fail on the basics. A business with clear processes, clean data, connected tools, a willing team, and a specific goal can put AI to work quickly. A business missing those pieces usually gets more value from fixing them first. The assessment scores five areas:

  • Processes: whether the work is documented and done consistently. You cannot automate a process nobody can describe.
  • Data: whether customer and operational data lives in one place and is clean enough to trust.
  • Tools and integrations: whether your apps can share information through integrations or APIs.
  • People and ownership: whether the team is open to change and someone owns the project.
  • Goals and guardrails: whether you know what problem you are solving and how AI may use your data.

How the score works

Each answer is worth 0 to 3 points. Your total is converted to a score out of 100, and each area gets its own percentage so you can see where to focus. The two lowest areas are highlighted with practical next steps.

What to do with your result

Whatever your score, the next step is the same shape: pick one specific, high-volume process, fix whatever blocks it, and automate it end to end. Use the priority scorer to choose the process, and the free Automation 101 and AI at Work 101 courses to build the skills.
faq: What is an AI readiness assessment?

A short evaluation of whether a business has the processes, data, tools, people, and goals in place to adopt AI and automation successfully. It highlights gaps to close before investing, so projects deliver results instead of stalling.
How do I know if my business is ready for AI?

You are ready for a first project if you can name a specific, repetitive process, the data it needs is in a system rather than in people's heads, your tools can connect, and someone has time to own it. You do not need a data science team or a large budget.
What should a small business do first with AI?

Start with one well-defined task where AI reads or writes language inside a workflow you already run: sorting incoming email, drafting replies for review, summarizing calls, or extracting data from documents. Keep a person reviewing anything customer-facing at first.
